pairs.source_text: Curribus Automedon lentisque erat aptus habenis, Tiphys in Haemonia puppe magister erat:
pairs.question: Quis in Haemonia puppe, qua Argonautae vecti sunt, magister erat?
pairs.question_en: Who was the helmsman on the Haemonian ship in which the Argonauts sailed?
pairs.derivation: Tiphys as the canonical helmsman of the Argo ('Haemonia puppis' = the Thessalian ship). Closed-book: standard Argonaut lore; anchored to the Argonauts. Single-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Curribus Automedon lentisque erat aptus habenis, Tiphys in Haemonia puppe magister erat: Me Venus artificem tenero praefecit Amori; Tiphys et Automedon dicar Amoris ego.
pairs.question: Qua arte excellebat Automedon, quem Ovidius cum Tiphye gubernatore componit?
pairs.question_en: In what skill did Automedon excel, whom Ovid pairs with the helmsman Tiphys?
pairs.answer_en: In driving the chariot (he was a charioteer).
pairs.derivation: Automedon, proverbial charioteer (canonically Achilles' driver), cited by Ovid as the master of chariot and reins. Closed-book canonical figure; answer supported by 'curribus lentisque aptus habenis'.

pairs.source_text: Phillyrides puerum cithara perfecit Achillem, Atque animos placida contudit arte feros.
pairs.question: Quis centaurus Achillem puerum citharam docuit?
pairs.question_en: Which centaur taught the boy Achilles the cithara?
pairs.derivation: Canonical myth: Chiron tutor of the young Achilles, here in music. 'Phillyrides' (son of Philyra) = Chiron, whom Ovid names explicitly five lines later ('Aeacidae Chiron'). Entity-anchored to Achilles; single-name answer.

pairs.source_text: Este procul, vittae tenues, insigne pudoris, Quaeque tegis medios, instita longa, pedes.
pairs.question: Cuius rei insigne erant vittae tenues feminarum Romanarum?
pairs.question_en: Of what were the thin headbands (vittae) of Roman women the badge?
pairs.derivation: Dress-code fact: the vitta was the mark of the respectable (chaste) woman, which is why Ovid banishes it from his poem. Stated verbatim ('insigne pudoris'). Culturally salient Roman costume knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Este procul, vittae tenues, insigne pudoris, Quaeque tegis medios, instita longa, pedes.
pairs.question: Quae pars vestis matronarum Romanarum pedes medios tegebat?
pairs.question_en: What part of the Roman matron's dress covered the middle of her feet?
pairs.derivation: The instita, the flounce sewn to the matron's stola reaching the feet, emblem of the married woman. Stated verbatim; canonical Roman dress fact.

pairs.source_text: Andromedan Perseus nigris portarit ab Indis, Raptaque sit Phrygio Graia puella viro,
pairs.question: Unde Perseus Andromedan portavisse dicitur apud Ovidium?
pairs.question_en: From where is Perseus said, in Ovid, to have carried off Andromeda?
pairs.derivation: Canonical Perseus-Andromeda rescue; Ovid places her among the Indi (elsewhere she is Ethiopian), so the question is attributed 'apud Ovidium'. Entity-anchored to Perseus and Andromeda; short place answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tu modo Pompeia lentus spatiare sub umbra, Cum sol Herculei terga leonis adit:
pairs.question: Cuius ducis Romani porticus umbram spatiantibus in Urbe praebebat, ut Ovidius commemorat?
pairs.question_en: The portico of which Roman general offered shade to strollers in the City, as Ovid records?
pairs.derivation: The Porticus Pompeia (attached to Pompey's theater), the famous shaded promenade of Rome, first in Ovid's catalogue of meeting-places. Venue fact, not advice; supported by 'Pompeia sub umbra spatiare'.

pairs.source_text: Tu modo Pompeia lentus spatiare sub umbra, Cum sol Herculei terga leonis adit:
pairs.question: Cuius herois leo inter signa caeli a poetis Romanis numeratur?
pairs.question_en: Which hero's lion do the Roman poets count among the signs of the heavens?
pairs.derivation: The zodiacal sign Leo identified as the lion of Hercules (the Nemean lion): the sun 'approaches the back of Hercules' lion' in high summer. Shared astronomical-mythological lore; supported by 'Herculei terga leonis'.

pairs.source_text: Nec tibi vitetur quae, priscis sparsa tabellis, Porticus auctoris Livia nomen habet:
pairs.question: Quae porticus Romana auctoris sui nomen habet et priscis tabellis picta erat?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman portico bears its founder's name and was hung with old paintings?
pairs.derivation: The Porticus Liviae, named for its foundress Livia and known as a gallery of old pictures ('priscis sparsa tabellis'). Monument fact from the venue catalogue; both details verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quaque parare necem miseris patruelibus ausae Belides et stricto stat ferus ense pater.
pairs.question: Quibus Belides, Danai filiae, necem parare ausae sunt?
pairs.question_en: For whom did the Belides, the daughters of Danaus, dare to prepare death?
pairs.answer_en: For their cousins (the sons of Aegyptus).
pairs.derivation: Canonical Danaid myth: the fifty daughters of Danaus ('Belides', from grandfather Belus) slew their cousin-bridegrooms. Anchored to the Belides; 'patruelibus' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quaque parare necem miseris patruelibus ausae Belides et stricto stat ferus ense pater.
pairs.question: Quis in porticu Danaidum Romae stricto ense stans effictus erat?
pairs.question_en: Who was represented standing with drawn sword in the portico of the Danaids at Rome?
pairs.derivation: The statue program of the Danaid portico (by the Palatine temple of Apollo): the daughters and their fierce father with drawn sword. 'Pater... stricto ense' verbatim; the father of the Belides is by canon Danaus.

pairs.source_text: Nec te praetereat Veneri ploratus Adonis, Cultaque Iudaeo septima sacra Syro.
pairs.question: A qua dea ploratus est Adonis?
pairs.question_en: By which goddess was Adonis mourned?
pairs.derivation: Canonical myth behind the Adonia rites (kept by women at Rome, hence a meeting-day in Ovid's catalogue): Venus mourning her Adonis. 'Veneri ploratus Adonis' verbatim; single-name answer.

pairs.source_text: Nec te praetereat Veneri ploratus Adonis, Cultaque Iudaeo septima sacra Syro.
pairs.question: Quoto quoque die Iudaei sacra sua colunt, ut Ovidius significat?
pairs.question_en: Every how many days do the Jews keep their rites, as Ovid indicates?
pairs.derivation: The Jewish sabbath ('septima sacra' of the 'Syrian Jew') observed at Rome, listed among the regular gathering-days. Ethnographic-religious fact, culturally salient in Augustan Rome; 'septima sacra' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec fuge linigerae Memphitica templa iuvencae: Multas illa facit, quod fuit ipsa Iovi.
pairs.question: Quae dea Aegyptia, cuius templa Romae frequentabantur, apud Ovidium 'linigera iuvenca Memphitica' dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Which Egyptian goddess, whose temples were much frequented at Rome, is called in Ovid the 'linen-clad Memphian heifer'?
pairs.derivation: Isis, whose devotees wore linen (linigera) and whose cult came from Memphis, identified with the heifer Io once loved by Jove ('quod fuit ipsa Iovi'); her Roman temple a noted women's haunt. The epithet-identification is standard ambient knowledge; distinct from the Io metamorphosis facts taken from Met. 1.

pairs.source_text: Subdita qua Veneris facto de marmore templo Appias expressis aera pulsat aquis,
pairs.question: Iuxta cuius deae templum marmoreum fons Appias expressis aquis aera pulsat?
pairs.question_en: Beside which goddess's marble temple does the Appian fountain strike the air with its jetted waters?
pairs.derivation: Topographical fact: the Appiades fountain stood below the marble temple of Venus (Genetrix, by Caesar's forum), where the law-courts met. Verbatim 'Veneris... templo Appias'; short one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: Spectatum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsae: Ille locus casti damna pudoris habet.
pairs.question: Quam ob causam duplicem feminae ad ludos veniunt, secundum celeberrimum Ovidii versum?
pairs.answer: Ut spectent et ut ipsae spectentur.
pairs.question_en: For what twofold reason do women come to the games, according to Ovid's most famous line?
pairs.answer_en: To see, and to be seen themselves.
pairs.derivation: 'Spectatum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsae' — proverb-famous line on theater culture; the checkable point (the double purpose) is stated verbatim. Attributed to Ovid, so closed-book and anchored.

pairs.source_text: Primus sollicitos fecisti, Romule, ludos, Cum iuvit viduos rapta Sabina viros.
pairs.question: Quo rege ludos edente virgines Sabinae a Romanis raptae sunt?
pairs.question_en: Under which king, as he gave the games, were the Sabine maidens seized by the Romans?
pairs.derivation: The rape of the Sabine women at the first games, instituted by Romulus — foundational Roman legend, here the aetiology of theater-courtship. Anchored to Romulus and the Sabines; verbatim support.

pairs.source_text: Tunc neque marmoreo pendebant vela theatro, Nec fuerant liquido pulpita rubra croco;
pairs.question: Quae supra theatrum marmoreum Romanum ad umbram spectatoribus praebendam pendebant?
pairs.question_en: What hung above the Roman marble theater to give the spectators shade?
pairs.derivation: Ovid contrasts Romulus' rustic games with the theater of his own day: marble building with hanging vela. The awnings of the Roman theater are a canonical spectacle-culture fact; verbatim 'marmoreo pendebant vela theatro'.

pairs.source_text: Tunc neque marmoreo pendebant vela theatro, Nec fuerant liquido pulpita rubra croco;
pairs.question: Quo liquore pulpita theatrorum Romanorum rubra fiebant?
pairs.question_en: With what liquid were the stages of Roman theaters made red?
pairs.derivation: Roman stages were sprinkled with liquid saffron essence ('liquido... rubra croco') — a well-attested spectacle custom (cf. Propertius, Lucretius). Ovid's negation about early times presupposes the practice of his day.

pairs.source_text: Illic quas tulerant nemorosa Palatia, frondes Simpliciter positae, scena sine arte fuit; In gradibus sedit populus de caespite factis, Qualibet hirsutas fronde tegente comas.
pairs.question: Quibus e rebus facti erant gradus in quibus populus primis ludis Romuli sedit?
pairs.question_en: Of what were the tiers made on which the people sat at Romulus' first games?
pairs.derivation: The primitive theater of Romulus' games: leafy scenery from the Palatine woods and turf-built seating. Anchored to the first games of Romulus; 'de caespite factis' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dumque, rudem praebente modum tibicine Tusco, Ludius aequatam ter pede pulsat humum,
pairs.question: Cuius gentis tibicen modos primis ludis Romanis praebebat?
pairs.question_en: Of what nation was the flute-player who supplied the tune at the earliest Roman games?
pairs.derivation: The Etruscan origin of early Roman stage music: the tibicen at Romulus' games is 'Tuscus', matching the tradition (Livy 7.2) that ludiones and players came from Etruria. Verbatim 'tibicine Tusco'.

pairs.source_text: Nec te nobilium fugiat certamen equorum; Multa capax populi commoda Circus habet. Nil opus est digitis, per quos arcana loquaris, Nec tibi per nutus accipienda nota est: Proximus a domina, nullo prohibente, sedeto, Iunge tuum lateri qua potes usque latus;
pairs.question: In quo spectaculorum genere Romae viro licebat nullo prohibente proximum a femina sedere?
pairs.question_en: At which kind of Roman spectacle was a man free, with no one preventing it, to sit right next to a woman?
pairs.answer_en: In the Circus (at the chariot races).
pairs.derivation: Famous seating fact: unlike the theater, the Circus had no separation of the sexes — 'proximus a domina, nullo prohibente, sedeto'. A spectacle-culture fact every Roman carried; anchored to the Circus.

pairs.source_text: Et bene, quod cogit, si nolis, linea iungi, Quod tibi tangenda est lege puella loci.
pairs.question: Quae res in sedilibus Circi vicinos, etiam si nolint, iungi cogebat?
pairs.question_en: What on the Circus benches forced neighbors together, even unwilling?
pairs.derivation: The linea, the marked divisions of the narrow Circus seating, pressed spectators against each other 'by the law of the place'. Realia of Circus seating, stated verbatim ('cogit... linea iungi').

pairs.source_text: At cum pompa frequens caelestibus ibit eburnis, Tu Veneri dominae plaude favente manu;
pairs.question: Quales deorum effigies in pompa Circensi ferebantur?
pairs.question_en: Of what material were the images of the gods carried in the Circus procession?
pairs.derivation: The pompa circensis opened the races with ivory statues of the gods borne in procession ('caelestibus... eburnis'). Canonical rite of the games; short material answer, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hos aditus Circusque novo praebebit amori, Sparsaque sollicito tristis harena foro.
pairs.question: Quo loco Romae, teste Ovidio in Arte Amatoria, harena ad munera gladiatoria spargebatur?
pairs.question_en: Where in Rome, on Ovid's testimony in the Ars Amatoria, was sand strewn for gladiatorial shows?
pairs.derivation: Gladiatorial munera were still given in the Forum in Ovid's day, the ground strewn with sand ('sparsa... harena foro'). Venue fact of spectacle culture; attributed to Ovid.

pairs.source_text: Dum loquitur tangitque manum poscitque libellum Et quaerit posito pignore, vincat uter,
pairs.question: Quo pacto spectatores muneris gladiatorii de victore inter se certabant?
pairs.question_en: In what way did spectators at a gladiatorial show contend with one another over the winner?
pairs.derivation: Betting custom at the munus: spectators staked a pignus on which fighter would win ('posito pignore, vincat uter'), consulting the libellus (program). Spectacle-culture realia, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid, modo cum belli navalis imagine Caesar Persidas induxit Cecropiasque rates?
pairs.question: Quarum gentium rates Caesar Augustus in spectaculo belli navalis imagine commisit?
pairs.question_en: Of which nations were the ships that Caesar set against each other in his staged naval battle?
pairs.derivation: The naumachia of 2 BC, in which Augustus re-enacted a sea-fight of 'Persian' and 'Athenian' (Cecropian) fleets — the battle of Salamis (cf. Res Gestae 23). Anchored to Caesar (Augustus) and the mock sea-battle; both fleet names verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Parthe, dabis poenas: Crassi gaudete sepulti, Signaque barbaricas non bene passa manus.
pairs.question: Cuius ducis Romani signa in barbaras Parthorum manus venerant?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman commander's standards had fallen into the barbarian hands of the Parthians?
pairs.derivation: The standards lost by Crassus at Carrhae, held by the Parthians — the grievance behind the projected Parthian expedition. Celebrated historical fact; 'Crassi... signaque barbaricas... manus' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tergaque Parthorum Romanaque pectora dicam, Telaque, ab averso quae iacit hostis equo. Qui fugis ut vincas, quid victo, Parthe, relinquis?
pairs.question: Quo more Parthi equites tela in hostes iaciunt?
pairs.question_en: In what manner do Parthian horsemen hurl their missiles at the enemy?
pairs.answer_en: While fleeing, from a turned-away horse.
pairs.derivation: The famous 'Parthian shot': the Parthians fight by feigned flight, shooting backwards from the retreating horse ('ab averso quae iacit hostis equo... qui fugis ut vincas'). Ethnographic fact every Roman knew.

pairs.source_text: Ergo erit illa dies, qua tu, pulcherrime rerum, Quattuor in niveis aureus ibis equis.
pairs.question: Quot et qualibus equis dux Romanus triumphans per Urbem vehitur?
pairs.question_en: By how many horses, and of what kind, is a Roman general borne through the City in triumph?
pairs.derivation: The triumphator's chariot drawn by four white horses, the general in gold — canonical triumph imagery; 'quattuor in niveis aureus... equis' verbatim. Anchored to the Roman triumph as institution.

pairs.source_text: Ibunt ante duces onerati colla catenis, Ne possint tuti, qua prius, esse fuga.
pairs.question: Quo habitu duces capti in triumpho Romano ante currum victoris incedunt?
pairs.question_en: In what state do captured leaders march before the victor's chariot in a Roman triumph?
pairs.answer_en: With their necks laden with chains.
pairs.derivation: Triumph procession fact: enemy leaders led in chains before the chariot. 'Ibunt ante duces onerati colla catenis' verbatim; canonical spectacle of the triumph.

pairs.source_text: Hic est Euphrates, praecinctus harundine frontem: Cui coma dependet caerula, Tigris erit.
pairs.question: Quo insigni effigies fluminis Euphratis in pompa triumphali noscebatur?
pairs.question_en: By what mark was the effigy of the river Euphrates recognized in a triumphal procession?
pairs.answer_en: By its brow wreathed with reeds.
pairs.derivation: Triumphs paraded personified effigies of conquered rivers; the Euphrates was shown reed-crowned. Practice-fact of the triumph (the invented-names advice around it is dropped); verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hic est Euphrates, praecinctus harundine frontem: Cui coma dependet caerula, Tigris erit.
pairs.question: Cuius fluminis effigiei in pompa triumphali coma caerula dependebat?
pairs.question_en: Which river's effigy in the triumphal procession had dark-blue hair hanging down?
pairs.derivation: Companion fact: the Tigris personified with sea-blue hair among the triumphal images. Anchored to the named river; 'cui coma dependet caerula, Tigris erit' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hos facito Armenios; haec est Danaeia Persis: Urbs in Achaemeniis vallibus ista fuit.
pairs.question: Unde Persis apud Ovidium 'Danaeia' vocatur?
pairs.question_en: Why is Persia called 'Danaeian' in Ovid?
pairs.answer_en: From Danae, the mother of Perseus.
pairs.derivation: The Greek eponymy the epithet rests on: the Persians traced their name to Perseus, son of Danae — hence 'Danaeia Persis'. Closed-book canonical genealogy; attributed to Ovid for the epithet.

pairs.source_text: Luce deas caeloque Paris spectavit aperto, Cum dixit Veneri 'vincis utramque, Venus.'
pairs.question: Quae dea iudicio Paridis ambas aemulas formae vicit?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess, by the judgment of Paris, defeated both her rivals in beauty?
pairs.derivation: The judgment of Paris: Venus victorious over the other two goddesses ('vincis utramque, Venus'). Canonical myth, verbatim support; Ovid's point that Paris judged in daylight is the frame.

pairs.source_text: Nocte latent mendae, vitioque ignoscitur omni, Horaque formosam quamlibet illa facit.
pairs.question: Quo tempore mendae formae latent, ut notissimo versu ait Ovidius?
pairs.question_en: At what time do beauty's blemishes lie hidden, as Ovid says in a very famous line?
pairs.derivation: 'Nocte latent mendae' — proverb-famous Ovidian tag on lamplight and wine deceiving the judgment of beauty. The checkable point (night hides flaws) is verbatim; attributed to Ovid.

pairs.source_text: Quid referam Baias, praetextaque litora velis, Et quae de calido sulpure fumat aqua?
pairs.question: Quod litus Campanum, velis praetextum, aquis de calido sulpure fumantibus notum erat?
pairs.question_en: Which Campanian shore, fringed with sails, was famous for waters smoking with hot sulphur?
pairs.derivation: Baiae, the resort on the bay of Naples, with its hot sulphur springs ('de calido sulpure fumat aqua') and sail-fringed shore. Celebrated leisure geography; both details verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ecce suburbanae templum nemorale Dianae Partaque per gladios regna nocente manu:
pairs.question: Quo modo regna sacerdotii in templo nemorali Dianae suburbanae (Aricinae) parabantur?
pairs.question_en: How was the 'kingship' of the priesthood at the grove-temple of suburban Diana (at Aricia) obtained?
pairs.answer_en: By the sword, with a guilty hand.
pairs.derivation: The rex Nemorensis: the priest-king of Diana's grove at Nemi near Aricia won his office by killing his predecessor ('parta per gladios regna nocente manu'). Famous Roman cult curiosity; the Arician identification is standard ambient knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Byblida quid referam, vetito quae fratris amore Arsit et est laqueo fortiter ulta nefas?
pairs.question: Cuius amore vetito Byblis arsit?
pairs.question_en: With forbidden love for whom did Byblis burn?
pairs.derivation: Canonical myth of Byblis' incestuous passion for her brother Caunus (told at length in Met. 9, not yet mined). 'Vetito... fratris amore' verbatim; the Ars adds the noose variant of her end.

pairs.source_text: Myrrha patrem, sed non qua filia debet, amavit, Et nunc obducto cortice pressa latet:
pairs.question: Quem Myrrha, non qua filia debet, amavit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Myrrha love, though not as a daughter ought?
pairs.derivation: Canonical Myrrha myth: unnatural love for her father (Cinyras), ending in her transformation into the myrrh tree ('obducto cortice pressa'). Verbatim support; single short answer.

pairs.source_text: Illius lacrimis, quas arbore fundit odora, Unguimur, et dominae nomina gutta tenet.
pairs.question: Cuius puellae nomen guttae odorae, quibus unguimur, servant?
pairs.question_en: Whose name do the fragrant drops with which we anoint ourselves preserve?
pairs.derivation: Aition of myrrh: the perfume-drops are the tears of Myrrha weeping from the scented tree, and 'the drop keeps its mistress's name'. Etymological-mythical fact that survives translation (the perfume is named for her).

pairs.source_text: Nota cano: non hoc, centum quae sustinet urbes, Quamvis sit mendax, Creta negare potest.
pairs.question: Quot urbes insula Creta sustinere dicitur?
pairs.question_en: How many cities is the island of Crete said to hold?
pairs.derivation: The Homeric epithet of Crete of the hundred cities, repeated as shared lore ('centum quae sustinet urbes'). Number fact, anchored to Crete, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nota cano: non hoc, centum quae sustinet urbes, Quamvis sit mendax, Creta negare potest.
pairs.question: Quo vitio Creta proverbio apud veteres notata erat?
pairs.question_en: For what vice was Crete proverbially marked among the ancients?
pairs.derivation: The proverbial mendacity of the Cretans ('quamvis sit mendax... Creta'), a Greek commonplace naturalized in Latin. Checkable point of a proverb; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: It comes armentis, nec ituram cura moratur Coniugis, et Minos a bove victus erat. Quo tibi, Pasiphae, pretiosas sumere vestes? Ille tuus nullas sentit adulter opes.
pairs.question: Cuius regis coniunx Pasiphae tauri amore capta est?
pairs.question_en: Of which king was Pasiphae the wife when she was seized with love for the bull?
pairs.derivation: Canonical Cretan myth: Pasiphae, wife of Minos, in love with the bull ('Minos a bove victus erat'). Anchored to both names, both in the quoted lines.

pairs.source_text: Hanc tamen implevit, vacca deceptus acerna, Dux gregis, et partu proditus auctor erat.
pairs.question: E qua materia facta erat vacca ficta, qua taurus a Pasiphae amatus deceptus est?
pairs.question_en: Of what material was the false cow made by which the bull loved by Pasiphae was deceived?
pairs.derivation: The wooden cow (Daedalus' device) specified as maple ('vacca... acerna'); the offspring (the Minotaur) betrayed the deed ('partu proditus'). Specific material fact, verbatim; anchored via the Pasiphae story.

pairs.source_text: Et modo se Europen fieri, modo postulat Io, Altera quod bos est, altera vecta bove.
pairs.question: Quo animali vecta est Europa?
pairs.question_en: On what animal was Europa carried?
pairs.derivation: Canonical myth: Europa carried over the sea on the bull (Jupiter). 'Altera vecta bove' verbatim; the paired Io-as-cow fact is left to the Metamorphoses 1 file already authored.

pairs.source_text: Cressa Thyesteo si se abstinuisset amore (Et quantum est uno posse carere viro?), Non medium rupisset iter, curruque retorto Auroram versis Phoebus adisset equis.
pairs.question: Quid Phoebus fecisse dicitur ob nefas domus Thyesteae?
pairs.answer: Currum retorsit medioque itinere ad Auroram rediit.
pairs.question_en: What is Phoebus (the Sun) said to have done on account of the crime of Thyestes' house?
pairs.answer_en: He turned his chariot back and returned to the dawn in mid-course.
pairs.derivation: The Sun reversing his course at the horror of the house of Thyestes (Aerope's adultery and its sequel, Atreus' feast) — canonical Pelopid myth. 'Curruque retorto... versis equis' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Filia purpureos Niso furata capillos Pube premit rabidos inguinibusque canes.
pairs.question: Quis Niso regi purpureos capillos furata est?
pairs.question_en: Who stole the purple lock of hair from king Nisus?
pairs.derivation: Canonical myth: Scylla betrayed her father Nisus by stealing his purple lock. 'Filia... Niso furata capillos' verbatim; the daughter of Nisus is by canon Scylla (Ovid here conflates her with the sea-monster Scylla — noted, not asked).

pairs.source_text: Qui Martem terra, Neptunum effugit in undis, Coniugis Atrides victima dira fuit.
pairs.question: Cuius victima periit Atrides Agamemnon, qui bellum et mare effugerat?
pairs.question_en: Whose victim was Agamemnon, son of Atreus, who had escaped war and sea?
pairs.derivation: Canonical: Agamemnon, having survived Troy and the sea, slain by his wife. 'Coniugis Atrides victima' verbatim; Clytemnestra is the canonical referent of 'coniugis'.

pairs.source_text: Cui non defleta est Ephyraeae flamma Creusae, Et nece natorum sanguinolenta parens?
pairs.question: Quo exitio periit Creusa Ephyraea?
pairs.question_en: By what death did Creusa of Ephyra (Corinth) perish?
pairs.derivation: The Medea story: Creusa of Corinth (Ephyra, the old name) burned by Medea's poisoned gift, and the 'parent bloodied by the murder of her children' is Medea herself. The flame-death is verbatim; anchored to the named Creusa.

pairs.source_text: Flevit Amyntorides per inania lumina Phoenix:
pairs.question: Cuius filius erat Phoenix, qui per inania lumina flevit?
pairs.question_en: Whose son was Phoenix, who wept through empty (blinded) eyes?
pairs.derivation: Patronymic fact: Phoenix (Achilles' old tutor) was son of Amyntor, blinded by his father in the canonical story. 'Amyntorides... Phoenix' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hippolytum pavidi diripuistis equi.
pairs.question: Quo modo Hippolytus periit?
pairs.question_en: How did Hippolytus die?
pairs.answer_en: Torn apart by his panicked horses.
pairs.derivation: Canonical end of Hippolytus: his terrified horses tore him apart ('pavidi diripuistis equi'). Short, verifiable, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid fodis inmeritis, Phineu, sua lumina natis? Poena reversura est in caput ista tuum.
pairs.question: Quorum lumina Phineus effodit?
pairs.question_en: Whose eyes did Phineus gouge out?
pairs.derivation: Phineus blinding his own (innocent) sons, a punishment that returned on his own head (his blindness) — canonical myth. 'Fodis inmeritis... sua lumina natis' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Fertilior seges est alienis semper in agris, Vicinumque pecus grandius uber habet.
pairs.question: Ubi seges semper fertilior est, ut proverbio ait Ovidius?
pairs.question_en: Where is the crop always more fertile, as Ovid says proverbially?
pairs.derivation: Proverb-famous couplet ('the grass is greener'): the crop richer in another's field, the neighbor's herd with fuller udder. The checkable point is verbatim and attributed.

pairs.source_text: Tum, cum tristis erat, defensa est Ilios armis: Militibus gravidum laeta recepit equum.
pairs.question: Quibus gravidus erat equus ligneus quem Ilios laeta recepit?
pairs.question_en: With what was the wooden horse pregnant which Troy joyfully received?
pairs.derivation: The Trojan horse 'pregnant with soldiers' ('militibus gravidum... equum'), received by rejoicing Troy. Canonical shared story; verbatim support.

pairs.source_text: Tu licet incipias qua flebilis Allia luce Vulneribus Latiis sanguinolenta fluit,
pairs.question: Cuius fluminis dies apud Romanos flebilis habebatur, quod vulneribus Latiis sanguinolentum fluxerat?
pairs.question_en: The day of which river was held mournful among the Romans, because it had flowed bloody with Latin wounds?
pairs.derivation: The dies Alliensis, anniversary of the disaster on the Allia (the Gallic rout of 390 BC), marked unlucky in the Roman calendar — 'flebilis Allia... sanguinolenta'. Celebrated calendar-fact; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quaque die redeunt, rebus minus apta gerendis, Culta Palaestino septima festa Syro.
pairs.question: Quae festa, a Syro Palaestino culta, rebus gerendis minus apta habebantur?
pairs.question_en: Which festival days, kept by the Syrian of Palestine, were held less fit for doing business?
pairs.answer_en: The recurring seventh-day festival (the Jewish sabbath).
pairs.derivation: Second sabbath notice: the seventh-day festival of the 'Palestinian Syrian' as a day on which business is not transacted ('rebus minus apta gerendis') — the no-work character of the sabbath as seen from Rome. Distinct facet from the 1.75-76 observance pair.

pairs.source_text: Quid, quasi natali cum poscit munera libo, Et, quotiens opus est, nascitur illa, sibi?
pairs.question: Quo libamento dies natalis apud Romanos celebrari solebat?
pairs.question_en: With what offering-cake was a birthday customarily celebrated among the Romans?
pairs.derivation: The libum as the birthday cake of Roman custom ('natali... libo'), the peg of Ovid's joke about the girl who 'has a birthday' whenever gifts are wanted. The realia (birthday libum) kept, the satire dropped.

pairs.source_text: Cera vadum temptet, rasis infusa tabellis: Cera tuae primum conscia mentis eat.
pairs.question: Qua materia, rasis tabellis infusa, litterae amatoriae Romae scribebantur?
pairs.question_en: On what material, spread over smoothed tablets, were love-letters written at Rome?
pairs.derivation: Letter-writing realia: wax poured on planed wooden tabellae, the standard medium for (love-)letters. 'Cera... rasis infusa tabellis' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hectora donavit Priamo prece motus Achilles; Flectitur iratus voce rogante deus.
pairs.question: Cui Achilles corpus Hectoris prece motus donavit?
pairs.question_en: To whom did Achilles, moved by prayer, give back the body of Hector?
pairs.derivation: The ransom of Hector: Achilles yields the body to Priam's supplication (Iliad 24), cited as shared story. All three names in the verbatim line.

pairs.source_text: Littera Cydippen pomo perlata fefellit, Insciaque est verbis capta puella suis.
pairs.question: Quo perlata littera Cydippen fefellit?
pairs.question_en: Carried on what did a letter deceive Cydippe?
pairs.derivation: The Acontius and Cydippe story (from Callimachus): the oath-inscription on an apple trapped the unwitting girl by her own read-aloud words. 'Cydippen pomo perlata' verbatim; anchored to the named Cydippe.

pairs.source_text: Interea, sive illa toro resupina feretur, Lecticam dominae dissimulanter adi,
pairs.question: Quo vehiculo dominae Romanae toro resupinae per urbem ferebantur?
pairs.question_en: In what conveyance were Roman ladies carried through the city, reclining on a couch?
pairs.derivation: The lectica, the curtained litter in which women were borne reclining — daily-life realia named verbatim ('toro resupina feretur, lecticam dominae').

pairs.source_text: Munditie placeant, fuscentur corpora Campo: Sit bene conveniens et sine labe toga:
pairs.question: Quo in loco corpora iuvenum Romanorum exercitatione sole fuscabantur?
pairs.question_en: Where were the bodies of young Romans tanned by the sun in exercise?
pairs.derivation: The Campus Martius as the exercise-ground of Roman youth, where bodies were bronzed ('fuscentur corpora Campo'). Daily-life venue fact; the Campus without epithet is the Campus Martius.

pairs.source_text: Hippolytum Phaedra, nec erat bene cultus, amavit; Cura deae silvis aptus Adonis erat.
pairs.question: Quem iuvenem, nec bene cultum, Phaedra amavit?
pairs.question_en: Which young man, though not well groomed, did Phaedra love?
pairs.derivation: Canonical: Phaedra's passion for Hippolytus, cited by Ovid as proof that neglected looks can please. Both names verbatim; distinct fact from the death-pair at 1.338.

pairs.source_text: Ebrius, ecce, senex pando Silenus asello Vix sedet, et pressas continet ante iubas.
pairs.question: Quo animali vehi solet Silenus, senex ebrius Bacchi comes?
pairs.question_en: On what animal does Silenus, the drunken old companion of Bacchus, ride?
pairs.derivation: Canonical attribute: Silenus barely astride his sway-backed donkey in the Bacchic train. 'Silenus asello vix sedet' verbatim; single-animal answer.

pairs.source_text: Iam deus in curru, quem summum texerat uvis, Tigribus adiunctis aurea lora dabat:
pairs.question: Quibus feris iunctus currus Bacchi trahebatur?
pairs.question_en: By what wild beasts was the chariot of Bacchus drawn?
pairs.derivation: Canonical attribute of Bacchus: the tiger-drawn car (here in the Ariadne episode; the Ariadne-crown and Bacchus-finding facts are left to the Catullus 64 file already authored). 'Tigribus adiunctis' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nycteliumque patrem nocturnaque sacra precare, Ne iubeant capiti vina nocere tuo.
pairs.question: Quo cognomine Bacchus pater a sacris nocturnis appellatur?
pairs.question_en: By what cult name is father Bacchus called from his nocturnal rites?
pairs.derivation: The epithet Nyctelius (from Greek nyx, night) paired verbatim with 'nocturna sacra' — the god of the night festival invoked at drinking. Cult-title fact, like the Fasti's Verticordia pair; translatable as a name.

pairs.source_text: Blanditiasque leves tenui perscribere vino, Ut dominam in mensa se legat illa tuam:
pairs.question: Quo liquore convivae Romani verba blanda in mensa perscribere solebant, ut Ovidius docet?
pairs.question_en: With what liquid did Roman banqueters trace tender words on the table, as Ovid teaches?
pairs.derivation: Banquet custom: messages written on the tabletop in wine for the neighbor to read. The practice-fact is kept (attributed to Ovid), the seduction advice around it dropped.

pairs.source_text: Huic, si sorte bibes, sortem concede priorem: Huic detur capiti missa corona tuo.
pairs.question: Quid capiti convivarum in conviviis Romanis imponi solebat?
pairs.question_en: What was customarily placed on the heads of guests at Roman banquets?
pairs.derivation: The banquet garland, passed along and set on the head ('detur capiti missa corona'), with drinking-turns settled by lot ('si sorte bibes') — table realia of the convivium.

pairs.source_text: Occidit Eurytion stulte data vina bibendo; Aptior est dulci mensa merumque ioco.
pairs.question: Qua re periit Eurytion Centaurus?
pairs.question_en: By what did the Centaur Eurytion perish?
pairs.answer_en: By foolishly drinking the wine set before him.
pairs.derivation: Eurytion the centaur, undone by wine at the Lapith wedding (Odyssey 21 lore), cited as the warning example against drunken brawls. 'Occidit Eurytion... vina bibendo' verbatim; the centaur identification is canonical.

pairs.source_text: Conloquii iam tempus adest; fuge rustice longe Hinc pudor; audentem Forsque Venusque iuvat.
pairs.question: Quem Fors Venusque iuvant, ut proverbio ait Ovidius?
pairs.question_en: Whom do Chance and Venus favor, as Ovid says proverbially?
pairs.derivation: Ovid's erotic variant of the proverb 'fortune favors the bold' — 'audentem Forsque Venusque iuvat'. Checkable proverb-point, verbatim and attributed.

pairs.source_text: Iuppiter ex alto periuria ridet amantum, Et iubet Aeolios inrita ferre notos.
pairs.question: Quorum periuria Iuppiter ex alto ridere dicitur apud Ovidium?
pairs.question_en: At whose perjuries is Jupiter said, in Ovid, to laugh from on high?
pairs.derivation: 'Iuppiter ex alto periuria ridet amantum' — the proverb-famous tag that lovers' oaths go unpunished, the winds carrying them off void. Verbatim; distinct from the Met. 1 Stygian-oath facts.

pairs.source_text: Dicitur Aegyptos caruisse iuvantibus arva Imbribus, atque annos sicca fuisse novem, Cum Thrasius Busirin adit, monstratque piari Hospitis adfuso sanguine posse Iovem.
pairs.question: Quot annos Aegyptus sub Busiride imbribus caruisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: For how many years is Egypt said to have gone without rain under Busiris?
pairs.derivation: The Busiris story: nine rainless years before the seer's remedy of sacrificing a stranger to Jove. Number fact anchored to Egypt and Busiris; 'annos sicca fuisse novem' verbatim; 'dicitur' keeps the story-frame.

pairs.source_text: Cum Thrasius Busirin adit, monstratque piari Hospitis adfuso sanguine posse Iovem. Illi Busiris 'fies Iovis hostia primus,' Inquit 'et Aegypto tu dabis hospes aquam.'
pairs.question: Quis primus a Busiride Iovi hostia factus est?
pairs.answer: Thrasius, ipse vates qui id piaculum monstraverat.
pairs.question_en: Who was the first to be made a victim to Jove by Busiris?
pairs.answer_en: Thrasius, the very seer who had prescribed the sacrifice.
pairs.derivation: The point of the exemplum: Busiris made the adviser Thrasius the first stranger-victim of his own rite. Both names verbatim; the poetic justice is Ovid's stated fact ('fies Iovis hostia primus').

pairs.source_text: Et Phalaris tauro violenti membra Perilli Torruit: infelix inbuit auctor opus.
pairs.question: Cuius membra Phalaris tyrannus tauro torruit?
pairs.question_en: Whose limbs did the tyrant Phalaris roast in the bull?
pairs.answer_en: Perillus's, the very maker of the bull.
pairs.derivation: The bronze bull of Phalaris of Acragas: its inventor Perillus was its first victim ('infelix inbuit auctor opus'). Celebrated tyrant-anecdote; both names verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Iustus uterque fuit: neque enim lex aequior ulla est, Quam necis artifices arte perire sua.
pairs.question: Qua lege nihil aequius esse ait Ovidius?
pairs.answer: Ut necis artifices arte sua pereant.
pairs.question_en: Than what law does Ovid say none is more just?
pairs.answer_en: That the contrivers of death perish by their own art.
pairs.derivation: Proverb-famous sententia drawn from the Busiris and Phalaris exempla; the checkable point (the maxim and whose it is) is verbatim and attributed to Ovid.

pairs.source_text: Turpe, nisi hoc matris precibus tribuisset, Achilles Veste virum longa dissimulatus erat.
pairs.question: Qua veste Achilles, matris precibus obsecutus, virum dissimulavit?
pairs.question_en: In what garment did Achilles, yielding to his mother's prayers, disguise his manhood?
pairs.derivation: Achilles hidden on Scyros in women's dress at Thetis' entreaty — canonical episode ('matris precibus... veste virum longa dissimulatus'). Anchored to Achilles; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Saepe 'mane!' dixit, cum iam properaret Achilles; Fortia nam posita sumpserat arma colo. Vis ubi nunc illa est? Quid blanda voce moraris Auctorem stupri, Deidamia, tui?
pairs.question: Quae virgo regalis in Scyro Achillem virum esse comperit?
pairs.question_en: Which royal maiden on Scyros discovered that Achilles was a man?
pairs.derivation: The Scyros episode: Deidamia, the king's daughter ('virgo regalis', 'Scyrias puella' just above), and Achilles. Named verbatim; canonical mother-of-Neoptolemus story.

pairs.source_text: Quid facis, Aeacide? non sunt tua munera lanae; Tu titulos alia Palladis arte petas. Quid tibi cum calathis? clipeo manus apta ferendo est: Pensa quid in dextra, qua cadet Hector, habes?
pairs.question: Cuius herois dextra Hector casurus erat?
pairs.question_en: By which hero's right hand was Hector to fall?
pairs.derivation: Canonical Iliad fact restated by Ovid: the right hand of Achilles ('Aeacide... in dextra, qua cadet Hector') will slay Hector. Both parties named; short name answer.

pairs.source_text: At non Actorides lectum temeravit Achillis: Quantum ad Pirithoum, Phaedra pudica fuit.
pairs.question: Quis heros, Actorides dictus, fidus Achilli sodalis fuit?
pairs.question_en: Which hero, called 'Actorides' (descendant of Actor), was Achilles' faithful companion?
pairs.derivation: Actorides = Patroclus (grandson of Actor through Menoetius), the loyal-friend exemplum who 'did not defile Achilles' bed'. Canonical patronymic identification; anchored to Achilles.

pairs.source_text: Hermionam Pylades quo Pallada Phoebus, amabat, Quodque tibi geminus, Tyndari, Castor, erat.
pairs.question: Quis Helenae Tyndaridi geminus frater erat, ut Ovidius refert?
pairs.question_en: Who was the twin brother of Helen, daughter of Tyndareus, as Ovid relates?
pairs.derivation: Ovid makes Castor the twin of Helen ('tibi geminus, Tyndari, Castor') — kinship fact of the Tyndarid family, attributed to Ovid since traditions pair the twins variously. Verbatim support.

pairs.source_text: Pallidus in Side silvis errabat Orion, Pallidus in lenta naide Daphnis erat.
pairs.question: Cuius puellae amore Orion pallidus in silvis errabat?
pairs.question_en: For love of which girl did Orion wander pale in the woods?
pairs.derivation: Side, Orion's beloved (his wife in the mythographers), a name-fact stated verbatim. Less celebrated but shared mythographic knowledge; anchored to Orion.

pairs.source_text: Pallidus in Side silvis errabat Orion, Pallidus in lenta naide Daphnis erat.
pairs.question: Cuius amore Daphnis pastor pallidus fuit?
pairs.question_en: For love of whom was the herdsman Daphnis pale?
pairs.derivation: Daphnis, the Sicilian herdsman of bucolic song, wasting for love of a naiad — canonical pastoral myth; 'in lenta naide Daphnis' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Utque leves Proteus modo se tenuabit in undas, Nunc leo, nunc arbor, nunc erit hirtus aper.
pairs.question: Quis deus marinus modo in undas, modo in leonem arboremve aprumve se mutare fingitur?
pairs.question_en: Which sea god is imagined turning himself now into water, now into a lion, a tree, or a boar?
pairs.derivation: Proteus the shape-shifter, with the canonical list of his transformations. Verbatim support; single-name answer.
